name: Sertoli cell tumour of the testis
aliases: large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour

clinicalPearls: Sertoli cell tumour is a sex cord-stromal tumour that is usually benign, though a small proportion, more often in adults, are malignant
It typically presents as a painless testicular mass and may be hormonally active, most commonly producing oestrogen and causing gynaecomastia
Germ cell tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG) are normal, helping to separate it from germ cell tumours

The large cell calcifying variant shows characteristic calcification on ultrasound, can be bilateral or multifocal, and is associated with genetic syndromes such as Carney complex and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
Assessment for an associated syndrome is warranted, especially with bilateral or calcifying tumours or a suggestive family history
Small benign-appearing lesions may be treated with testis-sparing surgery, while radical inguinal orchidectomy is used when malignancy is suspected
Histological features such as larger size, necrosis, vascular invasion, and increased mitoses suggest malignant potential and prompt staging and follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Sertoli cell tumours arise from the Sertoli cells that normally support spermatogenesis within the seminiferous tubules. Neoplastic Sertoli cells may aromatise androgens to oestrogen, producing hyperoestrogenic effects such as gynaecomastia and, in children, endocrine disturbance. The large cell calcifying subtype, characterised by prominent calcification, occurs in the context of tumour-predisposition syndromes including Carney complex and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Most tumours are indolent and benign, but a minority display features associated with metastatic behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Germ cell tumour of the testis
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound, noting calcification and multifocal or bilateral lesions
Serum AFP and beta-hCG (normal) to exclude a germ cell tumour
Hormonal profile including oestradiol and testosterone when endocrine features are present
Evaluation for Carney complex or Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with calcifying or bilateral tumours
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis if malignancy is suspected
Histological assessment of malignancy-associated features and margins
redFlags: Large or rapidly enlarging tumour with malignant histological features
Evidence of metastatic spread on staging
Bilateral or calcifying tumours signalling an underlying tumour-predisposition syndrome
Marked hyperoestrogenic features such as progressive gynaecomastia
reference.prognosis: Most Sertoli cell tumours are benign and cured by excision; malignant variants, predominantly in adults, respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and carry a guarded outlook once metastatic, while identification of an associated syndrome has implications for lifelong surveillance.
pitfalls: Missing an associated Carney complex or Peutz-Jeghers syndrome in a patient with calcifying or bilateral tumours
Assuming a hormonally active mass is benign without assessing malignancy-associated features
Performing orchidectomy for a small benign lesion amenable to testis-sparing surgery
Mistaking tumour calcification for benign microlithiasis
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Perform radical inguinal orchidectomy where malignancy is suspected, reserving testis-sparing surgery for small, benign-appearing lesions
Evaluate and manage hormonal effects such as oestrogen-driven gynaecomastia
Assess for associated tumour-predisposition syndromes, particularly with bilateral or calcifying tumours, arranging surveillance for Carney complex or Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
Stage malignant variants with cross-sectional CT imaging and manage metastatic disease surgically, since these tumours respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Undertake surveillance imaging and confirm normal germ cell markers to monitor for malignant behaviour
Refer to a urology and oncology multidisciplinary team and offer genetic counselling for syndromic tumours
